Mara kept lost things downstairs, in oak cabinets numbered by category and, more precisely, by degree of uncertainty. Buttons sat beside unfinished letters; umbrellas shared shelves with apologies never spoken. Mara’s favorite room contained scents: woodsmoke, oranges, chalk dust, her grandmother’s lavender soap. Each sat inside a glass bell jar, carefully labeled. Her supervisor, Mr. Vale, insisted that no object be guessed at too quickly. An uncertain thing was dangerous, he said. It might grow teeth. That warning had once been funny. No one laughed now, especially not at Drawer Thirteen, which was painted the same gray as the wall.

One November night, while rain tapped the windows like a patient visitor, Mara heard a sound in the cabinet corridor. Not a rattling drawer. Not a rolling marble. A soft, metallic cough. She found a brass key beneath the empty scent of rain. It was warm, finely made, and tagged with a paper label in her own handwriting. MARA’S—ROOM THIRTEEN. The ink glistened as though freshly applied. For as long as she could remember, the gray drawer had possessed neither lock nor keyhole. She only wished the key itself had possessed the decency to remain lost. The rain agreed.

Mr. Vale had left work early, muttering about a headache and carrying his umbrella upside down. Mara told herself that a peculiar key was simply a peculiar object, and peculiar objects belonged in the gray drawer, not in her evening tea. At midnight, however, the cabinet began breathing again. Drawers that had been shut all day slipped open one after another, releasing the whispers of a hundred misplaced things. A bicycle horn sounded in the basement. Somewhere, a tiny dog barked furiously. Then the gray wall clicked, and a narrow seam appeared around Drawer Thirteen. It exhaled pale, cold air.

She placed the key against the wall. The brass lock appeared beneath her fingers as if pushed up through paint. One turn, and Drawer Thirteen swung outward, becoming a door tall enough for a person and much taller for anything imaginary. Beyond it waited a spiral staircase descending into a blue darkness. Mara took her lantern, left a note for Mr. Vale, and descended. The stairs went farther than any basement should allow. On the walls, labels drifted past in reverse order: FIRST LESSON, LAST SUMMER, THE WORD FOR EVERYTHING, and finally, in tiny letters, BEFORE YOU WERE ALMOST AFRAID.

At the bottom stood a circular room lined with glass cases. Inside them were lives that had nearly happened. Mara saw herself learning to sail, kneeling in an unfamiliar kitchen, laughing beneath a sky of green fire. She saw versions of Bellweather: one drowned by moonlight, one crowded with machines that spoke in polite voices, one blooming with white flowers from every rooftop. In the center rested an open book. As Mara approached, its pages rustled with voices. Each page contained a day, complete down to its smallest sound, the scrape of a chair, a sigh, a dog barking fiercely.

A girl in a gray uniform sat reading by the book. She looked twelve, perhaps thirteen, with Mara’s eyes and her mother’s impatient chin. “You took your time,” she said. “I thought you might never come.” Mara stared. The girl smiled and introduced herself as Mara, too, which was confusing since the name already fitted Mara like an old coat. She explained that the city’s lost things included discarded possibilities. Bellweather made choices, selecting one future and forgetting all the rest. Drawer Thirteen stored the overlooked days so they would not swell up inside people’s dreams. Like dangerously wet paper.

Every year, the keeper had to visit one discarded day and surrender it for good. Otherwise, it began leaking into ordinary life. Cracks appeared in teacups. Strangers shared memories. People woke with songs in languages they had never learned. The girl opened the book to a page dated the ninth of May, twenty-three years earlier. Mara remembered it immediately: a bicycle beside the river, a stolen honey cake, rain beginning just as she and her father found a shelter. She had been eleven. She had been happy so fiercely that, years later, grief had worn the memory thin. Like glass.

“You don’t have to pretend it never mattered,” the girl said. “You only have to stop keeping it alive.” Mara touched the page. For a moment, she felt rain on her cheeks and heard her father laughing behind her. Then she let go. The day folded itself into the book and vanished. It did not hurt. It felt like setting down a heavy bag carried so long she had mistaken its weight for her own body. The cases around them brightened. Each vanished possibility became a little more solid, while the girl holding the book became pale, transparent, and terribly relieved.

When Mara opened her eyes, she was in her own bed. Morning light lay across the floorboards, and the rain had stopped. On her desk sat an envelope from Mr. Vale. He had found her note, he wrote. He did not ask where she had been. Below his signature was a postscript: “The umbrella was not mine. I believe you have misplaced it.” Mara laughed for a long time. Outside, morning brightened the windows. For the first time in years, she allowed herself to look forward to whatever came next, and found the old department felt more like a beginning.

On her way back to work, Mara found a new arrival waiting on the department steps. It was a tiny paper boat, smelling faintly of oranges. Its label read OWNER UNKNOWN, but someone had added beneath, in pencil, WILLING TO TRY. Mara smiled and pocketed the boat. It flexed gently with her steps, as if carrying a small, patient passenger: possibility, perhaps, or simply the beginning of a story. Time, she thought. By sunset, it occupied a sunny window drawer. Outside, buses sighed and shopkeepers called prices. Mara unlocked the heavy oak door that evening, ready to begin once more.
